claims.text: Coupling high-resolution DSC, high-temperature dilatometry, and configurational-entropy-corrected CALPHAD can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
The intended starting materials are single-phase, as-cast HEAs with disordered fcc or bcc lattices.
DSC detects a dramatic heat-capacity increase when the solidus temperature is reached.
DSC can measure the latent heat of fusion in the proposed HEAs.
High-temperature dilatometry can monitor the volume discontinuity at melting.
CALPHAD incorporating configurational-entropy corrections can interpret and extend the DSC and dilatometry measurements.
An inert or vacuum atmosphere avoids oxidation during the measurements.
Controlled heating rates permit clear resolution of thermal transitions from cryogenic temperatures through melting.
High configurational entropy in HEAs produces a homogenized Gibbs-free-energy landscape.
The configurational-entropy-mediated free-energy landscape enables mixing models and adjusted CALPHAD parameters to relate heat-capacity and expansion data to fusion properties.
Entropic stabilization of HEA phases modifies the relative enthalpic and entropic contributions to melting.
Low-temperature heat capacity follows Debye T^3 behavior, while near room temperature it approaches the Dulong-Petit value of 3R in the absence of magnetic or phase transitions.
Heat-capacity evolution and the latent-heat jump at the melting temperature can be used to derive fusion enthalpy and fusion entropy.
CALPHAD configurational-entropy corrections permit extrapolation and generalization of the measured observables across different HEA compositions.

For single-phase, high-symmetry HEAs, the integrated method will agree with CALPHAD predictions and literature values for melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change within approximately 5–10%.
The method can efficiently resolve thermodynamic properties despite HEA chemical complexity and sluggish diffusion.
DSC and dilatometry without CALPHAD integration generally provide only qualitative trends, whereas the integrated method improves quantitative accuracy and efficiency.
The approach is primarily applicable to entropy-stabilized, single-phase HEAs and is less reliable for multiphase or strongly segregated alloys whose phase contributions cannot be deconvoluted.
CALPHAD predictions for HEAs remain challenging for transformation temperatures, phase compositions, and phase fractions, even when substantial binary and ternary assessment data are available.

The approach is falsified if any predicted melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, or melting volume change differs from an independent measurement by more than 10% in single-phase HEAs, or if results are inconsistent across a representative HEA range.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis claims applicability across the high-entropy-alloy family, whereas the boundary restricts reliable applicability primarily to entropy-stabilized, single-phase HEAs and excludes or limits important multiphase and segregated portions of that family.
